title: The Breakthrough
reviewNotes: Four branches start in the physically reconstructed seven-piece position after b6/axb6 at 26s, kings h1/h3. c6/bxc6/a6/c5/a7/c4/a8=Q wins; an independently declined sacrifice also promotes. Immediate axb6 loses against best defense, while the independently checked automatic cxb6/cxb6 exchange gives a drawn b6/b7 wall instead. The earlier eight-piece b6 choice is source context.
transcript: Fools will resign, but wise players will know how to win with white from this position. This seems like a drawn end game because both players are left with three pawns each, but white has a specific idea to force one of his pawns through [snorts] the wall of the black pawns. And first move is pawn to B6, the most flexible of the options. Now black has to recapture with one of these two pawns, or on the next move we're going to take and promote. But after he does that, we are not actually going to take back that pawn because if we did after the recapture by black, there would be no way to make any progress. The white pawn is always going to be stopped by one of the black pawns, and if you take like this, there is no way to make any progress. Instead, white has the very tricky and surprising pawn to C6, sacrificing yet another pawn. But of course, if black does take this pawn, we now have created a path for this other white pawn to simply walk through the black pawns. And despite black having a majority of pawns, white is simply going to be the first one to promote to a new queen. And this is going to be a simple win. And the same thing would have happened if black had decided to take this pawn. Now, with this other pawn, we are able to take here, and black is just not in time to promote. We are going to get a queen and very easily win the game. If you like this board, read the pinned comment.
